# <span style="color:#E656AE;">Reproducible Research</span>

## C. elegans experiment {-}
*The data for this exercise was kindly supplied by J. Louter (INT/ILC) and was derived from an experiment in which adult C.elegans nematodes were exposed to varying concentrations of different compounds.*

First we load in the dataset. 

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
library(readxl)
CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata <- read_excel("~/CE.LIQ.FLOW.062_Tidydata.xlsx")
head(CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata)
```

You would expect the columns <span style="color:#E656AE;">RawData</span>, <span style="color:#E656AE;">compName</span> and <span style="color:#E656AE;">compConcentration</span> all to be numeric. These are the colums we are interested in. 

- <span style="color:#E656AE;">RawData</span> = the outcome - number of offspring counted as an integer value, after incubation time, 

- <span style="color:#E656AE;">compName</span> = the generic name of the compound/chemical 

- <span style="color:#E656AE;">compConcentration</span> = the concentration of the compound

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
# inspect the data types of colums RawData, compName and compConcentration
class(CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata$RawData)
class(CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata$compName)
class(CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata$compConcentration)
```

But in R the variable <span style="color:#E656AE;">compConcentration</span> is not 'numeric', it is of the data type 'character'. 

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# convert column compConcentration from character to numeric 
# Remove NA and convert to numeric 
library(dplyr)

CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata <- CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata %>%
  mutate(compConcentration = as.numeric(compConcentration)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(compConcentration))             
```


### Scatterplot {-}
Scatterplot of the data set for the different compounds and the varying concentrations down below:

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(
  data = CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata, 
  aes(x = log10(compConcentration), y = RawData)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = compName, shape = expType),
    size = 1.5, 
    alpha = 0.8,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.1)) + 
  labs(
    x = "log10(compConcentration) in nM",
    y = "RawData in counts")
```


<span style="color:#E656AE;font-weight:bold;">Figuur 3. Scatterplot of different compounds and varying concentrations</span>

The positive control for this experiment is <span style="color:#E656AE;">ethanol</span> and the negative control is <span style="color:#E656AE;">S-medium</span>.

### Normalizing the data {-} 

For the dataset CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata, the controleNegative condition was normalized so that its average value equals 1. All values are expressed as a fraction of this, which helps standardize the data and facilitates the interpretation and comparison of the effects of different conditions.

```{r}
# Calculate mean value of controlNegative
controlNegative <- CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata %>% filter(CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata$expType == "controlNegative")
controlNegative_mean <- mean(controlNegative$RawData) 
controlNegative_mean

# Normalize data
CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata <- CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata %>% mutate(normalized = CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata$RawData / controlNegative_mean)

# Inspect the data types of columns RawData, compName, expType, compConcentration and normalized
CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata %>% select(RawData, compName, compConcentration, expType, normalized)
```

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(
    data = CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata, 
    aes(x = log10(compConcentration), y = normalized))+
  geom_point(
    aes(color = compName, shape = expType),
    size = 1.5, 
    alpha = 0.8,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.1))+ 
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata",
    caption = "Data normalized with the negative control mean",
    x = "log10(compConcentration) in nM",
    y = "RawData in counts")
```


<span style="color:#E656AE;font-weight:bold;">Figuur 4. Scatterplot of different compounds and varying concentrations normalized with the mean of the negative control</span>

### Future Research {-}
To determine the effect of different chemicals on the _C. elegans_ model and its offspring, a dosis response analysis would be the next step. This would allow to calculate the IC₅₀ value, which is the concentration at which a compound reduces the offspring by 50%. The `drc` package in R is commonly used for this purpose. 

We begin by grouping data per compound and visualizing how offspring numbers vary by concentration. Then we fit a dose-response model to estimate the concentration at which the response (offspring count) drops by half --> the IC₅₀ value.


1. Installing the `drc` package 
```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("drc")
library(drc)
```

2. Filter the dataset for a specific compound and experimental conditions
```{r, eval=FALSE}
compound_data <- CE_LIQ_FLOW_062_Tidydata %>%
  filter(compName == "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", expType == "experiment")
```

3. Use a four-parameter log-logistic model
(This model estimates the relationship between the compound concentration and the biological effect (in our case, the normalized number of offspring). It assumes that the response follows a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve, which is typical in toxicology.)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
celegans <- drm(normalized ~ compConcentration,
             data = compound_data,
             fct = LL.4())
```

4. Calculate the data and summarize 
```{r, eval=FALSE}
summary(celegans)
ED(celegans, 50) 
```

5. Plot the dosis response curve
This visualizes the calculation of step 4. 
```{r, eval=FALSE}
plot(celegans, type = "all",
     xlab = "Concentration (µM)",
     ylab = "Normalized Offspring",
     main = "Dose-Response Curve for 2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene")
```

## Article {-}
An, A.Y. et al. (2023) Dynamic gene expression analysis reveals distinct severity phases of immune and cellular dysregulation in COVID-19, bioRxiv. Available at: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.11.04.565404v1.full (Accessed: 02 May 2024). 

### Summary {-}
Objective 
To investigate longitudinal changes in gene expression profiles throughout the COVID-19 disease timeline.

Methods 
Three-hundred whole blood samples from 128 adult patients were collected during hospitalization from COVID-19, with up to five samples per patient. Transcriptome sequencing (RNA-Seq), differential gene expression analysis and pathway enrichment was performed. Drug-gene set enrichment analysis was used to identify FDA-approved medications that could inhibit critical genes and proteins at each disease phase. Prognostic gene-expression signatures were generated using machine learning to distinguish 3 disease stages.

Results 
Samples were longitudinally grouped by clinical criteria and gene expression into six disease phases: Mild, Moderate, Severe, Critical, Recovery, and Discharge. Distinct mechanisms with differing trajectories during COVID-19 hospitalization were apparent. Antiviral responses peaked early in COVID-19, while heme metabolism pathways became active much later during disease. Adaptive immune dysfunction, inflammation, and metabolic derangements were most pronounced during phases with higher disease severity, while hemostatic abnormalities were elevated early and persisted throughout the disease course. Drug-gene set enrichment analysis predicted repurposed medications for potential use, including platelet inhibitors in early disease, antidiabetic medications for patients with increased disease severity, and dasatinib throughout the disease course. Disease phases could be categorized using specific gene signatures for prognosis and treatment selection. Disease phases were also highly correlated to previously developed sepsis endotypes, indicating that severity and disease timing were significant contributors to heterogeneity observed in sepsis and COVID-19.

Conclusions 
Higher temporal resolution of longitudinal mechanisms in COVID-19 revealed multiple immune and cellular changes that were activated at different phases of COVID-19. Understanding how a patient’s gene expression profile changes over time can permit more accurate risk stratification of patients and provide time-dependent personalized treatments with repurposed medications. This creates an opportunity for timely intervention before patients transition to a more severe phase, potentially accelerating patients to recovery.

## Reproducible data
In addition to reviewing scientific articles, the reproducibility of R code is also assessed in research papers. For this review, we examine the study by Kragness and Cirelli on infant behavior to evaluate various aspects, interactions, and emotional responses during a musical concert. The article used for this review is titled “A concert for babies: Attentional, affective, and motor responses in an infant audience.”

After studying the R script, it appears to be an analytical study of associations between different behavioral aspects during music playback. It performs statistical analyses, such as correlation tests, and generates visualizations. On a scale from 1 (very bad) to 5 (very good), I would rate the script a 4 for readability. The code is generally clear, well-structured, and organized with comments. However, it would benefit from additional comments that offer more detailed explanations of the code's functionality.

While running the script, I encountered a few minor errors. For example, when loading the data, the path was missing in the `setwd()` function. This was corrected by directing it to the folder named `'les4'`.

In the **Demographics** code chunk, the columns `Gender` and `BabyMusiClass` were not found as objects in the `df.wide` dataframe. I resolved the issue with `BabyMusiClass` by referencing it as `df.wide$BabyMusiClass`. The `Gender` column was stored as a *character* rather than a *factor*, which made counting values problematic. I adjusted this by using `table(df.wide$Gender)` to correctly display the gender counts in the console.

On a scale from **1 (very bad)** to **5 (very good)**, I would rate the script a **4** for **reproducibility**. The required changes were minor and easily implemented, such as correcting file paths or referencing variables explicitly. The visualizations were provided as PNG files, and all necessary libraries were loaded at the beginning of the RMarkdown file.

Below is an example of a code section used to generate a `geom_density` plot. This visualization gets a **5** for reproducibility.


```{r, eval=FALSE}
png("attentionDensity.png", units="in", width=5, height=5, res=300)

dens.perc <- ggplot(df, aes(BabyAttShow.Prop,fill = SongCond, linetype=IntCond),..scaled..) + geom_density(alpha = 0.2)+theme_classic()+
    scale_linetype_manual(values=c("solid", "dashed"))+
    scale_fill_manual(values=c("plum4","seagreen3"))+
    xlab("Proportion of epochs containing looks to show")+
  ylab("Kernel density")+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

dens.perc
dev.off()
```
